purpose: Primary-publication evidence and provenance audit for SCI1; not clinical validation or an exhaustive systematic literature search.
reviewDefinition: A primary URL is the original publisher, society, public-health body or bibliographic record. Reviews and consensus documents are not primary randomized trials. ReviewLevel records the content actually inspected.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand: Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.evidenceType: Society position stand; umbrella review of 137 systematic reviews
sources.reviewLevel: Full-text eligibility, interpretation and practical-recommendation sections inspected by the implementation reviewer, plus abstract and official ACSM interpretation; supplementary-review reappraisal not performed.
sources.accessLimits: One reader initially met an access wall; later primary PMC text was available. Supplemental review-level appendices were not independently reappraised.
sources.population: Healthy adults aged at least 18; over 30,000 participants; interventions 6–52 weeks; evidence search through October 2024.
supportedPrinciples: Progressive resistance training improves muscle function across adulthood.
Strength favors heavier loading, full range, 2–3 sets and at least twice-weekly training; hypertrophy responds to higher weekly volume.
Failure and complex periodization are not consistently necessary for improvement.
limits: Heavy-load optimization is not a universal novice starting prescription.
No exact Movefield exercise menu, RIR gate, set ramp, deload or template was tested.

sources.title: WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
sources.reviewLevel: Official publication record and age-group recommendations on WHO summary checked; complete guideline evidence tables not reviewed
sources.population: Children and adolescents 5–17, adults 18–64, and older adults 65+; recommendations also discuss specified clinical populations.
supportedPrinciples: Adults: 150–300 moderate or 75–150 vigorous aerobic minutes weekly, plus major-muscle strengthening on at least two days.
Youth: average 60 daily moderate-to-vigorous minutes, with vigorous, muscle- and bone-strengthening activity at least three days weekly.
Older adults additionally benefit from balance/strength multicomponent activity at least three days weekly.
limits: Whole-week health guidance is not validation of a lifting-only, brief or two-walk app program.
Special-population recommendations do not confer individual medical clearance.

sources.title: Resistance Training for Children and Adolescents
sources.evidenceType: AAP clinical report; expert synthesis and recommendations
sources.reviewLevel: Official indexed recommendation excerpts and reaffirmation notice checked; complete article not reviewed
sources.accessLimits: AAP full-text/PDF redirected to inaccessible SSO; PubMed was intermittent.
sources.population: Children and adolescents; resistance-training competence and qualified supervision are central.
supportedPrinciples: Begin with low intensity and 1–2 sets of 8–12 while learning.
Increase resistance gradually as technique and competence develop; instruction and supervision remain required.
limits: The report does not prescribe Movefield's fixed three-week 1×8 foundation or its exact staged second-set rule.
A supervision attestation does not assess technique; supervised 1RM testing is not universally prohibited by the report.

sources.title: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper from the National Strength and Conditioning Association
sources.evidenceType: NSCA position statement; expert evidence synthesis
sources.reviewLevel: Official full PDF retrieved; relevant program-design and progression sections reviewed
sources.population: Healthy children and adolescents; age-appropriate instruction and competent supervision.
supportedPrinciples: Start light; use 5–10 minutes of dynamic preparation, balanced movements and qualified supervision.
Typical strength work: 1–3 sets of 6–15; power work: 1–3 sets of 3–6.
Train 2–3 nonconsecutive days; gradual load progression responds to strength and technique.
limits: Older position statement, cross-checked against AAP's reaffirmed report.
Its ranges do not validate an exact app youth template or automatically assess recovery.

sources.title: Resistance Training for Older Adults: Position Statement from the National Strength and Conditioning Association
sources.evidenceType: NSCA position statement; evidence synthesis and recommendations
sources.reviewLevel: Official full PDF retrieved; general recommendations, progression and individual-adaptation sections reviewed
sources.population: Older adults with varied function, mobility, frailty and chronic-condition contexts.
supportedPrinciples: Work toward 2–3 sets for major muscles, 2–3 days weekly, with intensity and progression adapted to ability.
Function, technique, tolerance and relevant conditions guide selection; age alone does not set load.
limits: 70–85% 1RM recommendations describe progressively developed training, not everyone's initial load.
The statement does not establish suitability of every unmodified adult app template for every older person.

sources.title: The Resistance Training Dose Response: Meta-Regressions Exploring the Effects of Weekly Volume and Frequency on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gains
sources.reviewLevel: Publisher abstract and bibliographic record checked; complete paywalled paper not reviewed
sources.population: 67 studies; 2,058 participants; 79.1% male; mean age about 25.
supportedPrinciples: Greater weekly volume associates with greater gains and diminishing returns.
Fractional indirect-set accounting fit these data best; frequency effects were clearer for strength than hypertrophy.
limits: Group associations do not give a universal weekly increase ceiling or individual optimal dose.
The app's exercise-specific muscle coefficients and exact weekly set counts are estimates.

sources.title: Exploring the Dose–Response Relationship Between Estimated Resistance Training Proximity to Failure, Strength Gain, and Muscle Hypertrophy: A Series of Meta-Regressions
sources.reviewLevel: Publisher abstract and methodological caveats checked; complete paywalled paper not reviewed
sources.population: Resistance-training study participants with varied training status; exact demographic extraction not reviewed.
supportedPrinciples: Estimated RIR had a negligible relationship with strength gains; closer-to-failure sets associated with more hypertrophy.
limits: RIR was reconstructed from intervention descriptions, and models had modest fit.
This does not validate a precise 2–3 RIR default or a two-exposure readiness test.

sources.title: Effects of Resistance Training Performed to Repetition Non-failure on Exercise Performance in Healthy Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
sources.evidenceType: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of randomized trials
sources.reviewLevel: Open full article retrieved; methods, results and limitations reviewed
sources.population: 20 studies; 556 healthy adults; mean study ages 19.0–67.6; trained and untrained participants.
supportedPrinciples: Non-failure had a small dynamic-strength advantage; other pooled outcomes showed no significant differences.
limits: Definitions and volume protocols varied; samples were small and heterogeneous.
No significant difference is not proof that all non-failure doses are equivalent or optimal.

sources.title: Effect of Resistance Exercise on Body Composition, Muscle Strength and Cardiometabolic Health during Dietary Weight Loss in People Living with Overweight or Obesity: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
sources.evidenceType: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials; GRADE assessment
sources.reviewLevel: Primary indexed abstract and bibliography checked; full publisher/PMC paper not reviewed
sources.population: 25 randomized trials; 1,608 adults aged 18–65, BMI at least 25, undergoing dietary weight loss.
supportedPrinciples: Adding resistance exercise preserved fat-free mass, increased fat loss and improved strength; added scale-weight loss was not significant.
limits: Certainty differed by outcome: fat mass high, fat-free mass moderate, strength low.
Diet-plus-training evidence does not validate the app's twenty-minute walking add-on or supersets as weight-loss treatment.

sources.title: Couch to 5K running plan

publication.dateNote: No publication or last-review date was exposed on the accessed page.

sources.evidenceType: Official public beginner running program; not an app-validation trial
sources.reviewLevel: Full current NHS schedule checked against all nine recipe stages, including distinct sessions in weeks 5–6
sources.population: People beginning running; Movefield restricts this automatic pathway to adults.
supportedPrinciples: Three weekly runs with a rest day between; staged run/walk intervals and five-minute opening/closing walks.
The sequence ends at 30 minutes of continuous running.
limits: Source fidelity is not a guarantee of completing 5 km, injury prevention or individual readiness.
App-authored brief/hybrid walk–runs are separate from this sequence.

sources.title: Time-Efficient Training Approach as a Solution to Sedentary Occupational Health Risks
sources.evidenceType: NSCA Personal Training Quarterly educational article; narrative synthesis and examples
sources.reviewLevel: Official article's pairing, warm-up and recovery sections checked
sources.population: Busy working adults; examples draw on differing training populations.
supportedPrinciples: Paired exercises are a possible organization strategy; preserve suitable preparation and rest.
limits: Not a consensus statement or trial of Movefield's accessory pairs.
Its examples include failure-oriented methods; citing it does not require applying those methods.
sources.usage: Historical pre-SCI1 focus context; current adult superset selection uses ZHANG-2025-SUPERSET.

sources.title: Plyometric Exercises
sources.evidenceType: NSCA educational book excerpt from Developing Power
sources.population: Athletes using plyometric work for lower-body power.
supportedPrinciples: Account for jumps already performed in sport; emphasize movement mastery and purposeful dose.
limits: Not a trial of six or three weekly app landings.
Does not validate the app's 48/72-hour calendar buffers or guarantee recovery.

sources.title: Physical Activity and Your Weight and Health
sources.reviewLevel: Official page's activity, weight and individual-variation guidance checked
sources.population: Adults seeking overall health and healthy weight.
supportedPrinciples: Activity supports health; weight-management activity needs vary and healthy eating remains relevant.
Adult health guidance includes at least 150 moderate aerobic minutes and two strengthening days weekly.
limits: Does not establish sufficient weight-loss dose for a pair of ten-minute walks.
No outcome guarantee for a specific app or superset routine.

sources.title: Superset Versus Traditional Resistance Training Prescriptions: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis Exploring Acute and Chronic Effects on Mechanical, Metabolic, and Perceptual Variables
sources.reviewLevel: Open publisher article retrieved; methods, results and limitations checked. Direct PubMed retrieval was intermittent.
sources.population: 19 studies, 313 healthy participants, mostly young trained men; only three studies assessed chronic outcomes.
supportedPrinciples: Supersets can shorten sessions but generally increase perceived exertion; effects depend on pairing.
Chronic pooled estimates were similar, with limited evidence.
limits: Small samples, heterogeneity and restricted populations limit generalization.
Exact Movefield pairings/rests are not validated; no guaranteed time savings or fat loss.
sources.appScope: Current selected adult superset principle source; not youth guidance.

limits: No exact Movefield plan, focus overlay or modifier algorithm had independently measured outcomes in the verified sources.
Structural builds, target counts, schedule checks and source fidelity do not establish safety, clinical suitability, adherence or optimal outcomes.

Additional app bibliography entries are not silently upgraded to full-text review by inclusion in planEvidence.
